newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- January CPI focus of market.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- January CPI focus of market.

text.p: January's Consumer Price Index (CPI) was slated for release early Wednesday and was expected to set the tone for the remainder of a holiday-shortened trading week.

Last week producer prices were 0.3 percent lower and market players were optimistic that another tame reading on inflation was due from CPI. On average, economists expected the overall number to be up 0.3 percent and the "core" level -- excluding the volatile food and energy components -- to increase 0.2 percent.

"How long can this continue? The Fed's been standing on one foot since July with a bias toward tightening but still doesn't have a smoking inflationary gun," said John Williams, chief global markets economist at Bankers Trust Co.

Lacking one or two strong inflationary readings at the producer or consumer levels means the Fed is unlikely to move before its meeting in May, Williams said, "even though everyone knows the economy is expanding too rapidly."
"So what do you tell people, to go long for three months? I don't think so," Williams said. The Fed's policy-making arm next meets March 25 and again on May 20.

"CPI should not be a surprise. The market has already built in a fairly benign inflation picture, so in a sense there's probably more downside potential than upside," said Mark Pittman, bond fund manager at Marshall Funds.
Pittman said he expected the market would likely remain in the 6.5 percent to 6.75 percent range it has established in recent weeks.

"We're trending down toward the bottom of that range now, but I don't see us breaking out of it in the near future," Pittman said. Marshall Funds has about $4 billion in fixed-income assets under management.
While CPI wasn't expected to create much of a stir by Pittman, employment was the wild card he said he was watching. He saw a tangible threat of inflation in higher wages.

"I'd be astonished if we saw anything other than what's expected tomorrow. This looks to be a disappointing week in terms of bond volatility," said Fred Sturm, economist at Fuji Securities Inc. in Chicago.
The only possibility for a sharp market reaction was if people had taken long positions in the hope that CPI would confirm the weak reading producer prices showed last week, Sturm said.
Sturm said attention to Thursday's new home starts was a more meaningful figure than CPI, which was just a "grand ho-hum."
John Mueller, chief economist at Lehrman Bell Mueller Cannon Inc., also saw no surprises in the consumer price index with both the overall and core rates gaining 0.3 percent.

"The dog that didn't bark in this economic cycle was the cost of wages. The last time we were at this stage in the economic cycle wages were running about 6.0 percent higher and that's not happening in the current cycle, he said.
Mueller said defining unemployment can be tricky but that he looked at manufacturing employment for an accurate reading.

"It's manufacturing that supplies the high-paying jobs and that sector has seen about 330,000 jobs fall off in the last two years. These people generally get jobs again, but not at the high rate of pay they were getting," Mueller said.
That was helping to keep labor costs low, he added.
Mueller said the next figure the market had to absorb was new home starts on Thursday, which should show some bounceback from December's low reading.
